forces: Piano; the cycle was written for two-manual harpsichord
intro: Shelley Katz plays the Aria that opens the Goldberg Variations, BWV 988, a richly ornamented melody over a slow-moving bass. The same bass line supports thirty variations before the Aria returns.

sections.label: A · G major towards D major
sections.mNote: The bass descends beneath the decorated melody.

sections.label: B · Through E minor to G
sections.mNote: The bass moves through E minor back to G major.

sections.label: B′ · Second half repeated
sections.mNote: The minor-key passage returns before the final G-major cadence.

cues.title: Aria, descending bass
cues.text: The right hand plays the melody with trills and appoggiaturas. Below it, the bass descends G–F♯–E–D, one step per bar. Bach built the thirty variations that follow on this bass and its harmonies, and the ornamented melody belongs to the Aria alone.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, bars 1–4; Mutopia edition, https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=979. The cycle’s bass foundation is discussed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldberg_Variations.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Forkel’s anecdote, 1802
cues.text: In the story Forkel told in his 1802 biography, Count Keyserlingk could not sleep. Goldberg stayed in an adjoining room to play for him, and Bach supplied the variations. The count rewarded Bach with a golden cup filled with a hundred louis d’or.
cues.evidence: Johann Nikolaus Forkel, Bach biography (1802), anecdote quoted at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldberg_Variations. The commission story is disputed; the 1741 title page has no dedication to Keyserlingk.

cues.title: Repeat of the first half
cues.text: After a cadence in D major, the first half starts again on G. The slow descending bass returns beneath the decorated melody, and the sixteen bars are played a second time.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, bars 1–16 and first repeat; Mutopia edition, music ID 979. Both halves repeat in this recording.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Bach’s own copy of the print
cues.text: Balthasar Schmid printed the Aria and its variations in Nuremberg in 1741; the title page called for a harpsichord with two manuals. Bach’s own copy of the print, found in Strasbourg in 1974, adds fourteen canons on the Aria’s bass.
cues.evidence: Title page of the 1741 first edition (“vors Clavicimbal mit 2 Manualen”) and the Handexemplar discovered in 1974, now in the Bibliothèque nationale de France: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldberg_Variations. Netherlands Bach Society, notes on BWV 988: https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-988.

cues.title: Second half, move to E minor
cues.text: The second half begins over D and moves towards E minor. The melody keeps its ornaments, and the bass moves more. The cadence in E minor falls in bar 24, and the Aria closes in G major in bar 32.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, bars 17–32: E-minor cadence in bar 24 and G-major close in bar 32. Mutopia edition, music ID 979.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Anna Magdalena’s copy, c. 1740
cues.text: Anna Magdalena copied the Aria onto two blank pages of her music notebook. The book was begun in 1725, and the handwriting dates this entry to around 1740. It stands among the pieces collected and played in the Bach household.
cues.evidence: Christoph Wolff’s dating of Anna Magdalena’s copy, summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldberg_Variations, Publication section. The approximate date concerns the copy.

cues.title: Repeat of the second half
cues.text: After the G-major cadence the second half, bars 17–32, is repeated. Its E-minor passage returns, followed by the longer runs. The final G is held under a fermata in bar 32, with the melody turning around it in an ornament.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, second repeat of bars 17–32; final fermata and melodic ornament in bar 32. Mutopia edition, music ID 979.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: From D major back to G
transitions.from: A · G major towards D major
transitions.how: The first half closes on a D-major chord, with D in the bass. The repeat goes straight back to the opening G. The bass descends again G–F♯–E–D, and above it the right hand repeats its ornamented melody from the start.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, bar 16 and repeat to bars 1–4; Mutopia edition, music ID 979.

transitions.title: The bass moves on from D
transitions.to: B · Through E minor to G
transitions.how: The D-major cadence ends the first half for the second time. The next bar keeps D in the bass, then moves down to C, and the following bars turn towards E minor. The three-beat pulse continues unchanged, and the right hand keeps its elaborate ornaments.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, bars 16–24; Mutopia edition, music ID 979.

transitions.title: G major, then the second half
transitions.from: B · Through E minor to G
transitions.how: The second half closes in G major, with a fermata over the final bar. At the repeat the pianist goes back to bar 17 and the bass D, and the passage through E minor and the return to G major are played a second time.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, bars 17–32 and second repeat; Mutopia edition, music ID 979.

composer.epithet: Composer who supplied music for Leipzig’s churches for twenty-seven years and wrote a large body of keyboard music.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, were found in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. In his cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, one voice sings the psalmist’s plea while another sings a hymn in long notes above it.
